questions.question: Define a mixture and explain how it differs from a compound. Give two examples of each.
questions.expected_answer: A mixture is two or more substances mixed together but not chemically joined; each keeps its own properties, they can be in any proportion and can be separated by physical methods. In a compound the elements are chemically joined in a fixed ratio, the compound has new properties, and it can only be separated by a chemical reaction. Mixtures: air, sea water, soil, sand and iron filings. Compounds: water, table salt, carbon dioxide.

questions.question: Name the property used by each of the following methods and give one use of each: hand sorting, sieving, magnetic separation, gold panning.
questions.expected_answer: Hand sorting: size, shape or appearance; picking stones out of beans or sorting recyclables. Sieving: particle size; removing stones from builder's sand or lumps from flour. Magnetic separation: magnetism (iron, steel, nickel, cobalt); removing steel cans from mixed waste or iron filings from sand. Gold panning: density; separating heavy gold from lighter sand and gravel.

questions.question: Describe how you would separate a mixture of dried beans, iron filings, sand and salt, naming each method and explaining why filtration alone could not give pure salt.
questions.expected_answer: Remove the beans by hand or with a sieve, because they are large. Use a magnet (covered in plastic) to remove the iron filings. Add water and stir so the salt dissolves while the sand does not. Filter: the sand stays on the filter paper as residue and the salt solution passes through as filtrate. Evaporate the water from the filtrate to obtain salt crystals. Filtration alone cannot separate salt from water because dissolved salt particles are small enough to pass through the filter paper with the water.
